title: Your birthday review
hookLine: a yearly look back and ahead: Seneca met his own age in his trees, and the Stoics asked what they'd done with it
tomorrow: why did the Buddha tell his monks to stop walking in the rains?

cards: Old photos have a way of ambushing you: the haircut, the face, the friend you forgot you had. Seneca got ambushed by a house. He went out to his country place and found it falling apart.
He scolded the bailiff. The bailiff said it wasn't his fault; the house was just old. Seneca had built it.
Then the plane trees, bare and knotted. Water them, he said. The bailiff swore he did.
The trees were old. Seneca had planted them himself and watched their first leaves. And the house wasn't finished with him yet.

teach.b: Then, at the door, a bent old man. Who's this, Seneca asked. Don't you know me, said the old man.
I'm Felicio, the steward's boy. You used to bring me little toys. Writing to a friend, Seneca admits it: everywhere he turned at that house, he met his own age.
Here's what a Stoic does with a moment like that. Not panic, and not pretend.

teach.h: OLD AGE IS FULL OF PLEASURE.
teach.b: Seneca writes that old age is full of pleasure if you know how to use it, and that each day should be ordered as if it closed the line.
He suggests ending the day with a line from Virgil: I have lived. And he had a habit he learned from the philosopher Sextius.

teach.h: WHAT DID I CURE? WHAT DID I RESIST?
teach.b: Each night, Sextius asked himself: what bad habit have I cured today? What fault have I resisted? In what am I better?
Seneca says he does the same when the lamp is out, going over his whole day, hiding nothing from himself and passing over nothing.
A birthday review is that Stoic question, asked once a year instead of once a night. The trees will be older. So will the face in the doorway.
The review doesn't ask you to stop that. It asks what you did with the year, and what you'll do with the next.

how: Stoics like Seneca reviewed each day at night, asking what they had cured, resisted and improved. Some people keep a yearly version on their birthday, writing a page that looks back and then ahead.

o: a doctor's yearly checkup scheduled near the date you were born
a yearly look back and ahead, asked on the day you were born
a party where friends list everything they like about you

p: falling apart, though Seneca built it
bare and knotted; he had planted them
the steward's boy, now an old man
asked each night: what have I cured?

s: Seneca wrote that old age is something to hide from
he wrote that old age is full of pleasure if you know how to use it.
Seneca reviewed his whole day at night, after the lamp was out
he learned it from Sextius: what have I cured, resisted, improved?
a Stoic review is mainly a list of goals for the future
it starts by looking back: what did I cure, what did I resist, how am I better?

games.q: a friend's birthday review is a long list of resolutions and nothing else. what would Seneca's practice add first?
o: a look back: what did I cure, what fault did I resist, in what am I better?
nothing: the Stoics only looked ahead, since the past can't be changed.
more goals: a longer list shows you've taken the year seriously.
games.why: Sextius's questions look back at what was done. Seneca asked them every night; a birthday asks them about a whole year.

practice: Pick up something you've owned for years: a mug, a ring, a book with a cracked spine. Hold it for the whole sit and feel where it's worn. As you hold it, ask Sextius's three questions about this past year, one at a time.

wordCard.voice: Your birthday review: the Stoic evening questions, asked once a year on your birthday, looking back and then ahead.

orig.note: Latin: I have lived. Seneca borrows the line from Virgil for the end of each day.

carryVoice: Your line: another year. Seneca met his age at the door, and asked what he'd done with it. See you on day 1643.

sources.ref: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 12.1-9 (the crumbling country house, the plane trees, Felicio at the door; old age full of pleasure if one knows how to use it; each day ordered as if it closed the series; Virgil's 'I have lived')
Seneca, On Anger 3.36 (Sextius's nightly questions; Seneca reviews his whole day when the light is out)
